solutions.check: 29 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 27 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Female columnist in Athens for instance

definitions.text: Female columnist in Athens for instance

parts.words: Female columnist in Athens for instance
parts.note: not a woman journalist but a carved woman serving as a pillar, as on the Erechtheion porch on the Athenian Acropolis

explanation.surface: A Greek woman writes a newspaper column in Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Columnist' suggests a writer; here it means something that acts as a column, a sculpted female figure holding up a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a stone statue of a woman used as a supporting pillar in classical architecture.

clue.text: Seaman killed "pour encourager les autres" (Voltaire)

parts.note: Voltaire's Candide mocks the 1757 shooting of the British naval commander John Byng, done 'to encourage the others'

explanation.surface: A sailor was executed, as Voltaire put it, to encourage the others.
explanation.walkthrough: John Byng was shot on his own quarterdeck after losing Minorca; Voltaire's Candide coined the phrase about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Byng held the top naval rank of flag officer when he was executed.

clue.text: Mormon leader has rest disturbed by a lad

parts.note: Brigham Young led the Mormons to Utah

indicators.note: disturbed letters are thrown out of order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A church elder's rest is interrupted by a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Brigham Young led the Latter-day Saints to Utah in 1847; 'disturbed' is the anagram signal for the four-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy or young person is a kid, a juvenile.

clue.text: Artist gets bird in a bit of trouble

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird

indicators.note: letters in a bit of trouble are in a mess, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter finds a little bird in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a bit of trouble' reads as a phrase about the bird, but 'bit of trouble' is the anagram signal and 'in a' its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian master Tiziano Vecellio was a Renaissance painter.

clue.text: Primitive or modern calculator ?

parts.note: the primitive reading is counting on the fingers, the digits; the modern reading is an electronic machine working in binary digits

explanation.surface: A question about counting devices old and new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital' means using fingers as well as using digits, so it fits both a finger-counter and a modern machine.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic machine handling numbers as discrete digits, and also a person counting on their fingers.

clue.text: Top medal received in action

indicators.note: the medal is taken into the word for action, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a suit is a legal action brought in court
MM is the Military Medal, a British gallantry award

explanation.surface: A soldier is decorated for bravery shown in combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Action' looks military to match the medal, but it is a lawsuit. MM is the British Military Medal.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest point of a mountain or anything else is its peak.

clue.text: Sailor fellow's request for quiet time after noon before brewing tea

indicators.note: the quiet-time pieces are placed ahead of the rearranged tea

parts.note: sh is what you say to ask for silence
1 pm, one o'clock in the afternoon, written I PM

indicators.note: brewing stirs things up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor asks for some peace at lunchtime before making a cuppa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time after noon' is one o'clock in the afternoon, the numeral one written as the letter I; 'brewing' is the anagram signal for the tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone serving on the same vessel is a fellow crew member.

clue.text: Warship can turn up in Othello

indicators.note: the turned piece goes inside the word for Othello

parts.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading the word from bottom to top

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A battleship appears in a performance of Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn up' reverses the can in this down clue. A monitor was a low, heavily armed ironclad gunship, after the USS Monitor.
explanation.definitionFit: The USS Monitor gave its name to a class of shallow ironclad gunboats.

clue.text: So Isaacson, R, is put in this reference book

indicators.note: the son and the letter are placed inside the word meaning so

parts.note: thus means so
Isaac's son is Esau, in Genesis

explanation.surface: Someone instructs that an author and an initial be listed in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isaacson' looks like a surname; read it as Isaac's son, the brother of Jacob in Genesis. 'Put in' places him and the R inside the word for so.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of synonyms, such as Roget's, is a standard reference work.

clue.text: Price of a kingdom

parts.note: Shakespeare's Richard III cries 'My kingdom for a horse!', so the price offered for a kingdom is a horse to ride; split the answer after its first letter

explanation.surface: What would it cost to buy a whole realm?
explanation.walkthrough: Read as A MOUNT, the horse Richard III would trade his kingdom for; read whole, it is simply a sum, a price.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum or quantity of money is what a price is, and a steed to ride is a mount.

clue.text: Director gives one ball after mid-August

indicators.note: the one-and-ball pieces are placed following the letters from the month
mid- asks for the central letters of the month's name, its middle pair

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A film director throws a single party in the middle of summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mid' takes the middle two letters of AUGUST, GU. 'Director gives' is the definition: what a director gives is direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Direction or advice offered by someone in charge is what a leader provides.

clue.text: Bobadil's sound skill in a game like poker

indicators.note: sound tells us that the phrase spoken out loud gives the answer

parts.words: skill in a game like poker
parts.note: brag is a card game like poker, and skill at it is brag art

explanation.surface: A swaggering character is good at a card game like poker.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Bobadil is the boastful soldier in Ben Jonson's play Every Man in His Humour; the 's stands for 'is'. BRAG ART spoken out loud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bobadil is the stock literary example of a boaster who talks big about his deeds.

clue.text: Saint who served in a Massachusetts vineyard

definitions.text: Saint who served in a Massachusetts vineyard

parts.words: Saint who served in a Massachusetts vineyard
parts.note: the busy sister of Mary in Luke's Gospel, who served Jesus at table, shares her name with the island of ___'s Vineyard off Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A holy woman once worked on a wine estate in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: Two clues in one: the Gospel saint who served at table, and the island off Cape Cod named for her.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Testament saint famous for serving is Mary's sister, and Massachusetts has an island vineyard bearing her name.

clue.text: Worn by a horse in this race

definitions.text: Worn by a horse in this race

parts.words: Worn by a horse in this race
parts.note: a racehorse wears a light shoe on each hoof, and the same word names a race run for a prize cup

explanation.surface: A question about what a racehorse has on in a particular contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is both a racing horseshoe and a race whose prize is a piece of silver, such as the Queen's ___.
explanation.definitionFit: A light aluminium racing shoe has this name, and so does a race run for a silver trophy.

clue.text: Flying squirrel puts Henry in a quiet rage

indicators.note: Henry is placed inside the quiet rage

parts.note: p is piano, quiet in music
anger is rage
Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

explanation.surface: A gliding creature drives a king into silent fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A quiet rage' looks like a mood; it is P, the musical sign for quiet, plus a word for rage. The Australian flying phalanger is popularly called a flying squirrel.
explanation.definitionFit: The gliding marsupials of Australia are popularly called flying squirrels, though they are possums.

clue.text: Yours sincerely is your imitator

parts.note: the proverb says imitation is the sincerest form of praise, so whoever copies you is the most sincere admirer

explanation.surface: A letter signed off politely by someone who copies everything you do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yours sincerely' looks like a letter ending; it plays on the saying that imitation is the sincerest form of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A copier pays the sincerest compliment, by the proverb, so he is the one heaping on praise.

clue.text: Balance of rig needed on a French river

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another means placed above it

parts.note: to rig out is to equip
the Oise is a river in northern France

explanation.surface: A ship's tackle is wanted for sailing a river in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rig' suggests sailing, but it is a verb meaning to fit out.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of equal weight on both sides, an even poise, is equilibrium.

clue.text: Frightfully surprised, began to take in money

indicators.note: the word for began swallows the money, so one goes inside the other

parts.note: started means began
L stands for pounds, from the Latin libra, as in the sign for British money

explanation.surface: Someone shocked began accepting cash.
explanation.walkthrough: L, the pound sign's letter, goes inside STARTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken aback by fright, made to jump, as a sudden noise does.

clue.text: Friction worried 4? Rot!

indicators.note: worried letters are shaken about, so the pieces are rearranged

parts.note: 4 points to the answer of 4-down, the Venetian painter

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the idea that friction ever bothered the painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' mixes the 4-down answer with ROT. The OCR read the count as a stray 1.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing away by rubbing is the old physical sense of the word, as in gradual erosion.

clue.text: Ted's out to reorganise defence of old-time investors

indicators.note: reorganise asks for these letters to be arranged anew

parts.note: Ted's gives its letters with the s

explanation.surface: A financier is told to restructure the protection for old-fashioned shareholders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investors' are not shareholders but besiegers, who invest a town; Roman attackers locked shields overhead in a tortoise formation.
explanation.definitionFit: Roman soldiers advancing on a besieged town formed a shell of overlapping shields called the tortoise.

clue.text: French author of a Russian council

parts.note: the Duma is the Russian parliament or council
'of' is rendered as the possessive 's attached to the council

explanation.surface: A French novelist apparently belongs to a Moscow assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: The cold solve guessed PUMAS; that square is unchecked, and the clue plainly gives the author of The Three Musketeers, read as the Duma's.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Dumas wrote The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo.

clue.text: Old ensign

definitions.meaning: very old, belonging to times long past
an old word for a flag or standard-bearer, as Iago is Othello's

explanation.surface: A veteran flag-bearer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means very aged, and in Shakespeare it is a standard-bearer's rank, as Iago is Othello's.

clue.text: This licence from this justice, Shakespeare ?

definitions.text: This licence from this justice, Shakespeare ?

parts.words: This licence from this justice, Shakespeare ?
parts.note: the one adjective fits a writer's liberty with facts, a fitting comeuppance, and the Bard himself

explanation.surface: A question about the freedom a judge grants the Bard.
explanation.walkthrough: Three phrases share the word: a licence writers take, justice that fits the crime, and a description of Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers' liberty with facts, fitting retribution, and a description of verse all use this adjective.

clue.text: Returned by Valentine from Olivia's handmaid

definitions.text: Returned by Valentine from Olivia's handmaid

parts.words: Returned by Valentine from Olivia's handmaid
parts.note: in Twelfth Night Valentine comes back from Olivia's house bearing the reply her handmaid gave him, that she will see no suitor

explanation.surface: A line about a character in Twelfth Night coming back from a lady's maid.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 of Twelfth Night Valentine is not admitted to Olivia, and brings Orsino back only her maid's reply.
explanation.definitionFit: What a messenger brings back is a reply to the message he carried.

clue.text: Go for gold — what's the outlook?

definitions.meaning: to search for gold by digging or panning
the view or expectation of what lies ahead

explanation.surface: An athlete aiming for first place wonders about their chances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go for gold' looks like sporting ambition; it means hunting for the metal in the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold miner searching for a strike does this, and the word also means expectations for the future.

clue.text: Old John allowed the challenge to be taken up

parts.note: Shakespeare's Richard II calls him 'Old John of Gaunt', the Duke of Lancaster
let means allowed

explanation.surface: An old man permitted someone to accept a dare.
explanation.walkthrough: John of Gaunt was a 14th-century English duke, 'Old John of Gaunt' in Shakespeare's Richard II.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight threw down an armoured glove as a challenge, and his rival picked it up to accept.

clue.text: Pot-bearer? That's right

definitions.meaning: a three-legged stand for a pot or kettle by the fire
from the old saying 'as right as a ___', meaning perfectly fine

explanation.surface: Someone confirms a guess about who carries the pots.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition leans on the old British phrase 'right as a ___', meaning in perfect order.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripod stand holds a hot pan, and the phrase 'right as a' this means all is well.

clue.text: Cheered firmly when established

definitions.meaning: ... for, as a fan cheers on a team
fixed fast, like a plant whose roots have taken hold

explanation.surface: A crowd applauded heartily once the place was set up.
explanation.definitionFit: To root for a team is to cheer it on, and something firmly fixed in place is deep-set like a plant.

clue.text: Amuse oneself in a new constructive way

definitions.text: Amuse oneself in a new constructive way

parts.words: Amuse oneself in a new constructive way
parts.note: the verb meaning to refresh oneself with leisure, and with a hyphen the verb meaning to build something over again

explanation.surface: Advice to find a fresh and productive hobby.
explanation.walkthrough: One spelling covers two verbs: to take recreation, and to create anew.
explanation.definitionFit: To take leisure is to relax with pastimes, and to make again is to rebuild from scratch.
